known_final_diagnosis: Extrinsic compression of the duodenum between the superior mesenteric artery and the aorta was also seen (figures 2–4). clinician.trajectory_summary: A woman in her 40s with a history of anxiety-depressive disorder, GERD, and adolescent eating disorders (anorexia/bulimia) presented with a 3-month history of progressive weight loss (6 kg), post-prandial epigastric pain worsening at the end of meals, nausea, vomiting, and asthenia. On admission, she weighed 45 kg (BMI 14.69 kg/m²). Physical examination revealed abdominal tenderness with upper part guarding, marked epigastric regional pain, tympanitic sounds on percussion, normal bowel peristalsis, and no organ enlargement. Laboratory studies showed only mild indirect hyperbilirubinemia (Gilbert's syndrome) and a urinary tract infection. Imaging workup included an x-ray with Gastrografin showing significant gastric dilation compatible with Wilkie's syndrome, and a contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan demonstrating extrinsic compression of the duodenum between the SMA and aorta, with reduction in the retroperitoneal adipose pad and an aorto-mesenteric angle of less than 20° (normal 25-60°). Conservative management was initiated with a high-calorie semi-liquid oral diet and liquid oral nutritional supplements (600 mL, 1.5 kcal/mL). At 1-year follow-up, the patient's weight had increased to 50 kg (BMI 19.5 kg/m²) with significant symptom improvement: epigastric pain was reduced, post-prandial nausea and vomiting resolved, and CT imaging showed reduced gastric dilation.

Imaging evidence of gastric dilation compatible with Wilkie's syndrome on x-ray with Gastrografin

CT scan confirmation of SMA syndrome: extrinsic compression of the duodenum between the SMA and aorta, reduction in retroperitoneal adipose pad, and aorto-mesenteric angle less than 20° (normal 25-60°)

final.final_diagnosis: Superior Mesenteric Artery (SMA) Syndrome - Extrinsic compression of the duodenum between the superior mesenteric artery and the aorta
final.trajectory_summary: A woman in her 40s with a history of anxiety-depressive disorder, GERD, and adolescent eating disorders (anorexia/bulimia) presented with a 3-month history of progressive weight loss (6 kg), post-prandial epigastric pain worsening at the end of meals, nausea, vomiting, and asthenia. On admission, she weighed 45 kg (BMI 14.69 kg/m²). Physical examination revealed abdominal tenderness with upper part guarding, marked epigastric regional pain, tympanitic sounds on percussion, normal bowel peristalsis, and no organ enlargement. Laboratory studies showed only mild indirect hyperbilirubinemia (Gilbert's syndrome) and a urinary tract infection. Imaging workup included an x-ray with Gastrografin showing significant gastric dilation compatible with Wilkie's syndrome, and a contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan demonstrating extrinsic compression of the duodenum between the SMA and aorta, with reduction in the retroperitoneal adipose pad and an aorto-mesenteric angle of less than 20° (normal 25-60°). Conservative management was initiated with a high-calorie semi-liquid oral diet and liquid oral nutritional supplements (600 mL, 1.5 kcal/mL). At 1-year follow-up, the patient's weight had increased to 50 kg (BMI 19.5 kg/m²) with significant symptom improvement: epigastric pain was reduced, post-prandial nausea and vomiting resolved, and CT imaging showed reduced gastric dilation.

key_supporting_evidence.claim: Clinical presentation consistent with duodenal obstruction: weight loss, post-prandial epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, and asthenia
Severe malnutrition on admission: weight 45 kg, BMI 14.69 kg/m², with 6 kg weight loss over 3 months
Physical examination findings consistent with gastric outlet obstruction: abdominal tenderness with guarding, marked epigastric regional pain, tympanitic sounds, normal bowel peristalsis
Imaging evidence of gastric dilation compatible with Wilkie's syndrome on x-ray with Gastrografin

CT scan confirmation of SMA syndrome: extrinsic compression of the duodenum between the SMA and aorta, reduction in retroperitoneal adipose pad, and aorto-mesenteric angle less than 20° (normal 25-60°)
Conservative management with high-calorie semi-liquid diet and liquid oral nutritional supplements

Successful clinical response at 1-year follow-up: weight recovery to 50 kg (BMI 19.5 kg/m²), resolution of post-prandial nausea and vomiting, reduction in epigastric pain, and reduced gastric dilation on CT

ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.basis: Objective imaging findings (gastric dilation, duodenal compression, abnormal aorto-mesenteric angle) and anatomical abnormality documented on CT scan rule out purely functional etiology

ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.alternative: Peptic ulcer disease or GERD alone
ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.basis: Physical examination findings of tympanitic sounds and imaging evidence of gastric dilation with duodenal compression indicate mechanical obstruction rather than mucosal disease
Laboratory studies were unremarkable (no inflammatory markers documented), and imaging showed mechanical compression rather than mass or inflammatory changes
